analyses.title: A Probabilistic Approach to Event-Case Correlation for Process Mining
analyses.research_question: Can missing case identifiers in timestamped business-process events be reconstructed automatically, without requiring acyclic processes or external execution-time heuristics, by optimizing process-model conformance and activity-duration consistency?
analyses.methodology: The paper proposes EC-SA, a population-based simulated-annealing method that partitions a totally ordered set of timestamped, initially uncorrelated events into non-overlapping cases using an input process model. Its bilevel objective first minimizes alignment cost between candidate traces and the process model and then minimizes variance in activity execution times across cases. The authors evaluate the method by removing case identifiers from twelve public real-life event logs and attempting to reconstruct them under two conditions: using the original distinct traces as effectively perfect process knowledge and using models discovered by Split Miner or Inductive Miner. Accuracy is measured with log-to-log trace similarity and elapsed-time error, and the second experiment is compared with the prior DCI method, including execution time with a 24-hour timeout.

key_findings.finding: EC-SA can reconstruct a complete case assignment from an event stream without case identifiers, assigning every input event to exactly one case even when an event cannot be replayed as enabled by the process model.

With effectively perfect process knowledge, EC-SA achieved an average L2Lsim of 0.901 across the twelve evaluated real-life logs, corresponding to an average accuracy loss of about 10 percent, while average L2LSMAPE was 17.6 percent.
Replacing perfect process knowledge with mined process models reduced L2Lsim by 4.42 percent on average and increased L2LSMAPE by 16.67 percent on average relative to the first experiment.

Correlation quality depends materially on the quality of the process model: low precision creates more alternative replay possibilities, while poor fitness can prevent stricter correlation methods from assigning deviating events.
Against DCI using Split Miner models, EC-SA had better L2Lsim on most evaluated logs, although DCI achieved higher L2Lsim on three logs and lower L2LSMAPE on one log.
DCI required about four times the average execution time of EC-SA in the reported comparison and timed out at 24 hours on three logs.

The study provides direct evidence for latent case-identity reconstruction among structured business-process events, but it does not empirically study enterprise email/chat threads, cross-document textual coreference, or conversational continuity.
The method produces a hard partition in which each event belongs to one and only one case; it does not model partial, overlapping, or explicitly evolving matter identity as an output representation.

limitations: The approach requires an input process model and assumes that it has exactly one start activity and terminating conditions.
The temporal objective assumes that occurrences of the same activity tend to have similar execution durations across cases.
The stochastic search can miss the global optimum when the number of simulated-annealing steps is insufficient for a given model-log pair.
Correlation accuracy is sensitive to process-model fitness and precision.
Events that cannot be replayed as enabled by the process model are assigned randomly to an open case, which guarantees completeness but can introduce incorrect correlations.

The evaluation reconstructs case identifiers after deliberately removing them from already correlated event logs, rather than evaluating naturally ambiguous case identity observed prospectively in operational systems.
The paper studies structured process events identified mainly by activity and timestamp, not the semantic content of workplace emails, chats, or documents.
Each event is assigned to exactly one non-overlapping case, so the formulation does not represent an event as simultaneously or partially associated with several work matters.
The paper does not evaluate incremental online continuity as new communications arrive, nor explicit changes or merges in matter identity over time.
raw_claims: Event correlation addresses the problem of determining which events belong to the same process case when explicit case identifiers are missing.
EC-SA takes timestamped uncorrelated events and a process model as input and returns a correlated event log.
Every input event is assigned to one and only one case in the generated event log.
The first optimization objective minimizes misalignment between candidate traces and the supplied process model.
The second optimization objective minimizes activity execution-time variance across cases.
The method uses population-based simulated annealing to explore alternative event-to-case assignments.
When an event is not enabled in any open process execution, EC-SA randomly assigns it to an open case so that no event remains uncorrelated.
The evaluation uses twelve public real-life process event logs spanning domains including healthcare, finance, government, and IT service management.
The first experiment evaluates reconstruction using the original log's distinct traces as effectively perfect process knowledge.
The second experiment uses process models discovered with Split Miner and Inductive Miner and compares EC-SA with DCI.
Under perfect process knowledge, the reported average L2Lsim is 0.901 and average L2LSMAPE is 17.6 percent.
Imperfect process models reduce reconstruction accuracy relative to using the original distinct traces.
EC-SA outperforms DCI on most of the reported accuracy comparisons but not on every dataset and metric.
DCI takes roughly four times the average execution time of EC-SA in the reported experiment and exceeds the 24-hour timeout on three logs.
The authors identify incorporating event payload data and alternative forms of process knowledge as possible future improvements.
